claims.text: Corrosion resistance of duplex stainless steels in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications is primarily governed by microstructurally mediated selective passivation.
In DS2205, the BCC phase is less noble than the FCC phase, and phase-specific work-function differences can produce micro-galvanic corrosion.
The lower-work-function phase preferentially oxidizes to form a Cr- and Ni-rich protective film.
A Cr- and Ni-rich film formed by the more anodic phase minimizes subsequent localized galvanic corrosion.
DS2205 has a duplex microstructure containing BCC and FCC phases, with Laves phase also suggested as a possible constituent.
Controlled heat treatment or processing will adjust the phase distribution.
Increasing the fraction of the anodic phase that forms passivating oxides should improve corrosion resistance.
DS2205 has been studied in NaCl-KCl-MgCl2 molten salt at 450 °C and 650 °C.
A 3.5 wt.% NaCl aqueous solution is an alternative proposed test environment for the mechanism.
The BCC phase selectively forms a thin, adherent Cr- and Ni-enriched passivating film.
Selective passivation reduces effective anodic current and limits galvanic coupling with the more cathodic phase.
A stable, adherent oxide layer inhibits local dissolution and acts as a barrier to further corrosion.
An engineered duplex microstructure will have lower corrosion-current density and weight loss than untreated duplex steel.
XPS should detect a Cr- and Ni-rich passivation film localized on the initially more anodic phase.
Conventional untuned duplex stainless steel forms a less uniform or weaker passivation film than the engineered material.
The proposed mechanism requires oxygen and a chemical potential that supports mixed-oxide-film formation.
The mechanism may cease to operate in extremely reducing environments where passivation cannot occur.
The quantitative effect of phase-fraction modification and the contribution of work-function differences remain uncertain.
Processed and conventional samples will be exposed under identical conditions and compared using XPS or EDS, polarization measurements, weight loss, and SEM.
A lack of statistically significant corrosion reduction together with failure to form the predicted film, or corrosion behavior independent of microstructure, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The intervention proposes increasing the anodic, oxidation-prone phase as beneficial, whereas the cited molten-salt study attributes reduced galvanic susceptibility to a lower BCC-phase fraction. The evidence therefore points in the opposite direction from the proposed phase-fraction change.
